storm.summary_layperson: Clear, dry evening ahead for Greenwich Cove — nothing on radar and no storm risk tonight.
storm.local_effect_blurb: The Sound-air temperature gap is already down to about 4°F and keeps narrowing through the evening, so there's no meaningful marine-layer buffer left by sunset — though with no storms anywhere near tonight, that isn't expected to matter.
storm.detail_html:
Skies are sunny and dry across the region with no active NWS alerts. KOKX radar shows no echoes anywhere near Riverside, and instability is low — CAPE sits at just 140–230 J/kg through the forecast hours, an atmosphere that struggles to sustain convection even if something tried to form.

The Sound's usual protective marine layer is essentially out of play tonight. The air–water gap is only 4.5°F right now, already below the ~5°F threshold that marks a meaningful buffer, and it narrows further as the evening air cools faster than the 74°F water — dropping to roughly 2°F by 6 PM and going negative by 7 PM. In other words, even if a cell showed up, the cove wouldn't get much extra protection from it.

The good news is there's nothing to protect against. The most likely outcome for the 5–10 PM window is a quiet, dry evening for Riverside and Greenwich Cove, no different from surrounding inland towns — this is a night where the "Sound bubble" story simply doesn't apply because there's no storm to blunt.

What would change this call: the AFD flags a chance of showers and thunderstorms arriving late Wednesday into Thursday, well outside tonight's window. If a cell were to develop or track in from the west, radar and the arrival-prediction engine would pick it up — but as of this update there is nothing approaching.

wind.regime_label: Light gradient wind — no sea breeze, direction may wander

hourly.shift_note: light, backing toward NW near sunset
very light, may go fully variable (extrapolated)

wind.tactics_blurb: Light gradient wind out of the NW/NNW with no sea breeze building — expect puffy, shifty conditions with big swings rather than clean pressure. Favor the middle of the cove away from the shoreline lee, and treat this as a drifter-class evening that keeps easing toward dark.
wind.tactics_detail_html:
Tonight is a gradient-only day, not a sea-breeze day. The two-ingredient sea-breeze test needs both a land–water temperature gap of at least 5°F and a building thermal signal — the air–water differential is only 4.5°F and just 5% of coastal stations are showing southerly flow, so neither ingredient is met. That puts this window in Regime B-light: light synoptic wind, no thermal contribution, magnitude in the 3–7 kt range (`mean_speed_authoritative_kt` = 6.0 kt).

Direction is out of the NNW–NW quadrant, which in the cove's geography is the offshore-over-land case: gusty and puffy with oscillations that can run 15–30°, rather than the clean, steady flow you'd get from a due-S or SSW sea breeze. Best-average pressure in this direction tends to sit mid-cove, away from the immediate lee of trees and houses along the NW shore — favor the center of the course over hugging either shoreline.

Wind-field coherence is notably loose tonight: `direction_agreement` across the full station ensemble is just 0.43, with the inland cluster reading NNE, the eastern Sound reading ESE, and the western cove cluster (RYC included) reading N–NNW. That's a fragmented, weak-gradient field rather than one dominant flow — expect the direction at the line to wander more than usual, and don't be surprised if it doesn't behave like a clean, single-axis regime.

RYC itself is currently reading N at 8.9 kt (10-min avg 9.6, gusting 15.2), a bit livelier than the ensemble average — cove-specific ground truth should be trusted over the broader average. HRRR's own forecast direction (NNW, 332°) is close to what RYC is showing, so there's no meaningful model/obs divergence to flag here; this correction only matters on sea-breeze days anyway, and tonight isn't one.

The HRRR forecast only extends cleanly through about 7 PM tonight (fetch hours beyond that were unavailable); the 8–10 PM rows are extrapolated from the observed easing trend rather than modeled directly, so treat them as lower-confidence. Because there's no thermal engine to collapse at sunset, the wind won't die suddenly — it will simply keep easing the light breeze it already is. Fleet impact: 3–7 kt is drifter/light-air specialist territory, sliding toward fully variable and postponement-risk by 9–10 PM.

data_caveats: HRRR forecast hours beyond ~7:00 PM EDT (f05–f12) were unavailable this run — the 8:00–10:00 PM wind rows are trend-extrapolated, not model-forecast, and carry lower confidence.
Station direction agreement is low (0.43) across the ensemble — the regional wind field is fragmented (light and variable), not a single coherent flow.
